paragraphs.text: As society has developed, the role of design has shifted and changed in scope, scale and technique. For most of human history, products were designed and made by individuals for their own use or by craftsmen who made a limited number of items to sell or barter. After hundreds of years of this craft-based production of goods, the industrial revolution in the 19th century created particular occupations to support industrial manufacture. Design filled a necessary and increasingly important function in the mass production of goods. Designers in industry were given titles such as engineer, architect, draftsman, chemist and so on. However, what defined these new designers more than any other thing was their ability to imagine products that could be made in quantity through large-scale production, and specify realistic ways to create them.

For mass production, the risk of serious flaws in the finished item must be removed as far as possible. Therefore, with the shift from craft to industrial manufacture, the process of creation shifted in great part from the actual maker of the product to its designer, the person who was best able to anticipate and thus avoid potential imperfections before the goods were actually made. Much of the judgement, dexterity and care was therefore manifested in thought and intention at the design stage, rather than during its manufacture.

As the scale of production of modern industrial goods has increased in our society, the choices and decisions made by designers have increased in importance. Now, these decisions often have global impact. For example, an architect who specifies a particular type of aluminum-framed window for a skyscraper is making a decision not only about cost, appearance, usability, strength and safety, but also about an entire supply chain that provides those windows, from the raw materials needed to make the components through the various steps in the manufacturing, marketing and shipping of the product. The architect's specifications play a role in shaping demands placed on international mineral mining and petroleum production companies, glassmakers and trucking companies, to name but a few. The actions of all of these players will in turn affect the people working in mining, in factories, and many other points along the supply chain. They will also touch the lives of people in communities in which the mines, factories, and trucks are located or moving through, as well as of those who live around the landfill where the windows may end up as rubbish perhaps many years in the future. The designer's reach is vast. There are many effects, both intended and unintended, that spread from the choices the designer originally makes.

This is known as the 'ripple effect' — when one action causes a series of other actions to happen. Until the late 20th century, designers did not have to think much about this because their role used to be simpler. The designer was usually responsible for not much more than creating products that looked good and that met the specific financial and functional requirements of the problem at hand. Today however, design is increasingly being re-defined in light of issues such as climate change, shifts in ecosystem structure and function, and water scarcity, as well as human rights violations, among other issues. An acute awareness of the ripple effect is a result of growing understanding of impacts of products and of the need for companies to be accountable for these impacts — the positive and negative results — throughout their operations and supply chains.

Many corporate leaders are now showing an active interest in the design process of the goods their companies make or sell. This increased interest is due to a range of reasons, not least of which is the recognition that it is best to be ahead of potential government regulation, as well as activist pressures and public relations disasters. This perception also means that companies hiring design firms are more aware of the need for sustainability —the goal of not harming the environment or depleting natural resources. They must support the long-term ecological balance and recognise the importance of integrating these issues into core strategy, operations, and products. It will be up to the designer to make sure these factors are incorporated into new products that can be successfully marketed.

In the future, it will be increasingly necessary for the designer to recognise that we must use far fewer resources to meet far more people's needs since many resources are already in short supply. How can people's perceived needs and desires be reshaped and addressed so that what they want can be achieved? How can the designer put principles of sustainability into practice? Fortunately, work has already begun on this. Visionary individuals and organisations are making strides in design approaches, such as the 'green design' movement, which attempt to ensure that design uses more natural products sensitively. Similar work is under way on providing guidance for the production of raw materials and manufacturing that considers human rights issues, most notably including 'fair trade'; this ensures that workers and producers of raw materials receive a reasonable price for their product. Yet numerous challenges remain, ranging from fully incorporating social goals, such as improving the conditions of the workers who are perhaps growing, digging up or otherwise providing raw materials, to assessing the ecological friendliness of materials.
